title: Letter to Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC providing comments from FERC staff re the draft Resource Reports 1, 5, 10, and 11 for the planned Desert Southwest Expansion Project under PF26-9.

documents.name: DSWE_FERC Cmts on draft RRs 1,5,10,11.pdf
documents.text:
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
                                    WASHINGTON, D.C. 20426
                                  OFFICE OF ENERGY PROJECTS



                                                  In Reply Refer To:
                                                  OEP/DG2E/Gas Branch 3
                                                  Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC
                                                  Desert Southwest Expansion Project
                                                  Docket No. PF26-9-000

October 20, 2026

VIA FERC Service

Michael Langston
Vice President & Chief Regulatory Officer
Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC
1300 Main Street
Houston, TX 77002

Re:    Comments on Draft Resource Reports 1, 5, 10, and 11

Dear Mr. Langston:

        The enclosure contains the comments of the FERC staff on draft Resource Reports
1, 5, 10, and 11 for the planned Desert Southwest Expansion Project. The comments ask
for clarifications of discrepancies and identify missing information that will assist your
preparation of a complete application for the project. To facilitate review of the revised
draft resource reports, Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern) should
include a matrix that identifies the specific locations in the resource reports (i.e., section
and page number) where the information requested in these comments may be found.
File your response in accordance with the provisions of the Commission's Rules of
Practice and Procedure.

        Electronic filing is encouraged using the Commission’s eFiling system (see
https://ferconline.ferc.gov/eFiling.aspx). Be sure to prepare separate volumes, as outlined
on the Commission’s website at https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-04/CEII-
Filing-guidelines.pdf, and label all controlled unclassified information (CUI) as described
at https://www.ferc.gov/cui. Critical Energy Infrastructure Information (CEII) (e.g., plot
plans showing equipment or piping details) and privileged information (PRIV) (e.g.,
cultural resources material containing location, character, or ownership information; trade
secret information; proprietary information) are considered CUI. This information
should be filed as non-public and labeled as: “CUI//CEII” (18 CFR 388.113),
 “CUI//PRIV” (18 CFR 388.112), and as otherwise appropriate with other statutes for
labeling CUI (e.g., “CUI//CEII/SSI” and in accordance with 49 CFR 15.13 marking
requirements). All CUI should be filed separately from the remaining information, which
should be marked “Public.” For assistance with the Commission’s eFiling system,
please contact FERC Online Support at FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov, (866) 208-3676
(toll free), or (202) 502-8659 (TTY).

      Thank you for your cooperation. If you have any questions, please contact me at
202-502-6370.

                                               Sincerely,
                                               ANDREA             Digitally signed by
                                                                  ANDREA JENSEN

                                               JENSEN             Date: 2026.10.20
                                                                  12:45:59 -04'00'
                                               Andrea Jensen
                                               Environmental Project Manager
                                               Office of Energy Projects



Enclosure




                                           2
                                                                                  Enclosure
                    Desert Southwest Expansion Project (Project)
                                Docket No. PF26-9-000
                                       Comments



Resource Report 1

1.   Transwestern anticipates a “6-day per week, 10- to 12-hour day construction
     schedule (i.e., Monday through Saturday, 7am to 7pm). Depending on summer
     temperatures and the absence of daylight savings time in Arizona, there may be
     periods where workdays begin and end earlier.” Clarify if the work that could
     occur prior to 7 am or after 7 pm would be restricted to activities that must be
     continuous once initiated, or if it could be general construction activities, and
     include a list of these construction activities. If general construction activities
     could occur, clarify any other restrictions on the frequency, duration, and location
     of these activities (for example, a maximum end time and minimum start time;
     proximity to noise sensitive areas, or maximum number of days per week where
     activities could occur prior to 7 am or after 7 pm).

2.   Transwestern indicates that certain facility-related tasks may occur between 7 pm
     and 10 pm, such as “laydown yard use and occasional after-hour deliveries.”
     Clarify the laydown yard(s) where this may occur, as well as the associated
     activity(s).

3.   Section 1.3.3.1 mentions that new office/warehouse buildings would be built at
     each new compressor station yard. Clarify the source and annual volume of water
     that would be required for operation at each compressor station. As applicable,
     update Resource Report 2.

4.   In either Resource Report 1 or Resource Report 8, include a table of collocated
     portions of the mainline, similar to table 8A-13 for the laterals.

5.   As previously requested, and to confirm the Project objectives serving as the basis
     for evaluating alternatives, include a table of the existing or planned facilities that
     would be served by each delivery lateral, to the extent known (i.e., clarify the end-
     use facilities for each lateral, as well as associated contracted volumes of natural
     gas).


                                            1
 6.    Include additional justification for requesting a standard permanent right-of-way
      width of 60 feet. Identify specific physical conditions that require an expanded
      permanent right-of-way that exceeds the width used by other pipelines (i.e., 50
      feet).

7.    Section 1.4.1.2 states the “landowner will have the right to cultivate, work, plow,
      harvest and use the land so long as it does not hinder, conflict, or interfere with
      Transwestern’s surface or subsurface rights or disturb its ability to operate,
      maintain, and protect its facilities.” Include a description of any “surface or
      subsurface rights” to which Transwestern is referring that are not already
      stipulated in an easement agreement with the landowner.

8.    Section 1.5 states “Transwestern estimates that approximately 50 percent of the
      construction workforce will be hired locally in areas where construction occurs
      near major population centers. In rural counties with small populations,
      Transwestern estimates that approximately 5 percent of the construction workforce
      will be hired locally, with the remaining 95 percent temporarily relocating to
      [communities] near active construction sites for the duration of project
      construction.” Include an estimate of the percent of total Project workforce that
      would be hired locally.

9.    Section 1.5.1.2.6 states that “during the monsoon season (June 15 to September
      30) Transwestern will install appropriate temporary erosion controls immediately
      after initial disturbance of the soil…outside the monsoon season, temporary
      erosion controls will also be installed immediately after soil disturbance at all dry
      wash crossings, road crossings, residential areas, and other sensitive areas
      designated by Transwestern’s EI [environmental inspector] or representative”
      (emphasis added). The word “also” is absent from similar language in
      Transwestern’s Erosion Control and Revegetation Plan (ECRP) at section 5.1.
      Therefore, clarify if, outside of monsoon season, Transwestern proposes to only
      install temporary erosion controls at dry wash crossings, road crossings, residential
      areas, and “other sensitive areas.” If so, describe why Transwestern considers the
      measures of the FERC Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance
      Plan (Plan) at section IV.F to be technically infeasible, or unsuitable due to local
      conditions and explain how Transwestern’s proposed alternative measures would
      achieve a comparable level of mitigation.

10.   Section 1.5.1.2.6 states “temporary erosion controls will be properly maintained
      throughout construction (on a daily basis during the monsoon season).” Clarify:

                                            2
        a.    the proposed schedule for inspection and maintenance of temporary erosion
             controls outside of the monsoon season; and

       b.    why Transwestern considers the measures of FERC’s Plan at section
             II.B.13 to be unnecessary, technically infeasible, or unsuitable due to local
             conditions. Explain how those alternative measures would achieve a
             comparable level of mitigation.

11.   Section 1.5.1.2.10 “Transwestern may replace proposed HDD [horizontal
      directional drill] crossings with other trenchless methods.” Confirm that
      Transwestern would receive approval in writing from FERC prior to replacing
      proposed HDD crossings with other trenchless construction methods, as the effects
      are not equivalent.

12.   Remove language in section 1.5.1.2.12 that states “water sourcing and disposal
      associated with hydrostatic testing of the compressor stations will be the
      responsibility of the contractors building the facilities.” Volume and source of
      water required for hydrostatic testing of the compressor stations should be
      included in section 1.5.1.2.12 or in Resource Report 2. Water sourcing and
      disposal for all construction water needs to be analyzed in the Project
      environmental document.

13.   Include in tables 1.5-3 and 1.5-4 an estimate of the volume of water required for
      HDD and its likely source.

14.   Transwestern notes that it would conserve water “as much as practical” during
      hydrostatic testing by cascading water between test sections “where feasible.”
      Additionally, “where feasible,” water that does need to be released “may” be
      stored in tanks or lined ponds and used for dust control or hydroseeding. Given
      the limited water availability in portions of the Project area, clarify Transwestern’s
      commitments regarding conservation of water through cascading hydrostatic test
      water between sections and reuse of hydrostatic test water for dust control or
      hydroseeding. Include examples, including justification, of where/when these
      procedures would not be feasible.

15.   Include additional information about the water sources in tables 1.5-5 and 1.5-6 to
      clarify the type of proposed water source (e.g., groundwater, surface water,
      private, municipal). In providing estimates of water usage for the Project, include



                                             3
       all activities that would require freshwater (e.g., concrete truck washing, dust
      control).

16.   Include the status of purchase/lease agreements for the site locations of all planned
      meter and regulator stations.

17.   Clarify the number of parcels/miles of the Project that have pending
      environmental surveys and include the status.

18.   Assess whether the Project would conflict with the alignment of a future water
      importation pipeline in Hudspeth County identified by El Paso Water Utilities
      Public Service Board (see Accession No. 20260804-5177).

19.   In appendix 1E (Right-of-Way Width Rationale), according to the text, Scenario
      1C with topsoil segregation requires 14.5 feet for “surface material” (i.e.,
      “excavated/graded materials) plus an additional 25 feet of additional temporary
      workspace (ATWS) for topsoil storage. However, the right-of-way cross section
      for Scenario 1C depicts a combined 14.5- plus 25-foot portion of the right-of-way
      as all being used for topsoil storage. Also, the Scenario 1C cross section has two
      “edge of construction corridor” lines on the right side (and one on the left). Revise
      the Scenario 1C figure to clarify the “edge of construction corridor” and to clarify
      topsoil versus “surface material” storage requirements.

20.   Given scope/scale of the Insignia Estates (planned development of over 2,000
      residences and other infrastructure) and Torch Clean Energy Power Plant projects,
      as well as proximity to the planned Project, include these facilities in the Notable
      Projects Considered discussion in section 3.0 of appendix 1L.

21.   In appendix 1L, include a discussion of relevant existing or planned projects, if
      any, near each of the new compressor stations.

22.   In appendix 1L, include maps showing the locations of the “notable projects”
      described in section 3.

23.   Include a response to the comment of Robert Jones (Accession No. 20261009-
      5001) regarding a proposed 300-foot-wide restriction and effects on property
      access and future developments.




                                            4
 24.   Include a table with Transwestern’s requested modifications to the FERC Plan and
      Wetland and Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures (Procedures)
      which includes:

       a.    the measure for which Transwestern is requesting modification;

       b.    why site- or Project-specific justification for why Transwestern considers
             the measures to be technically infeasible, or unsuitable due to local
             conditions; and

       c.    an explanation for how Transwestern’s proposed alternative measures
             would achieve a comparable level of mitigation.

25.   In Transwestern’s adapted FERC Plan (Transwestern’s FERC Plan), the term “dry
      wash” was added as a change to the FERC Plan. Clarify why Transwestern
      appears to classify dry washes separately from other ephemeral waterbodies.

26.   In Transwestern’s FERC Plan and adapted FERC Procedures, Transwestern states
      “… playas are expected to be dry at the time of construction, they will be crossed
      using typical cross-country construction methods.” Revise Transwestern’s Plan
      and adapted FERC Procedures to clarify that typical cross-country construction
      methods are not acceptable where a playa has perceptible flow at the time of
      crossing or where a playa meets the criteria for a wetland under the current federal
      methodology for identifying and delineating wetlands.

27.   Transwestern’s FERC Procedures includes references to specific waterbodies.
      Revise or remove this text, as applicable, where route/siting modifications are
      incorporated in the Project application.

28.   Address the following regarding Transwestern’s ECRP (appendix 1G).

       a.    Section 1.0 states “The ECRP incorporates BMPs [best management
             practices] provided by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and erosion
             control and revegetation guidelines provided by the Natural Resources
             Conservation Service (NRCS) and various Soil and Water Conservation
             Districts.” Identify within the ECRP and in Transwestern’s table of
             proposed modifications to the FERC Plan and Procedures (refer to question
             24) where proposed revisions are based on recommendations from the
             BLM, NRCS, and Soil and Water Conservation Districts.



                                            5
 b.   Section 4.3.1 states “ATWS have been located at least 50 feet from the
     edge of dry washes, where feasible, based on topographic conditions or
     other constraints. As outlined in Transwestern’s FERC Procedures
     (V.B.2.a), the ATWS may be shifted to within 10 feet of the top bank of the
     dry wash crossings during construction when no water is present.” Section
     6.0 states “these shifts would not occur in Pima County where Floodplain
     Management Ordinance (Chapter 16.30) requires protection and
     mitigation.”

        i. Identify each ATWS that would be within 50 feet of dry washes and
           include a site-specific explanation of the circumstances and a
           detailed justification why a 50-foot buffer cannot be maintained.

        ii. Describe why Transwestern considers the measures of the FERC
            Procedures at section V.B.2 to be technically infeasible, or
            unsuitable due to local conditions and explain how Transwestern’s
            proposed alternative measures (i.e., shifting ATWS to be within 10
            feet of the top bank of dry wash crossings during construction when
            no water is present) would achieve a comparable level of mitigation.

c.   Section 4.3.2 states “where necessary, vegetation clearing will be
     completed by mowing, mulching, or scalping off the tops of shrubs…the
     surface soil, desert pavement, and cleared vegetation material will be left
     in-place, on the non-working side of the right-of-way.” Transwestern’s
     Resource Report 1 at section 1.5.1.2.5 describes similar measures but
     indicates salvaging and incorporating vegetative material into surface soil
     would be completed only in rangeland. Clarify this apparent discrepancy,
     as well as how this measure is consistent with section III.E of the FERC
     Plan (beneficial reuse) and indicate if this measure was recommended by a
     land managing agency and/or state resource agency.

d.   Section 4.3.2 states “during clearing operations, at dry wash crossings
     where woody shrub vegetation is dense, and the cleared vegetative material
     cannot be readily incorporated into the surface soil, the EI will determine
     where the cleared vegetation can be salvaged and stored on the edge of the
     construction right-of-way so that this vegetation debris can be respread as
     surface mulch after restoration on the wash banks to provide cover for
     small mammals and reptiles along these movement corridors until
     vegetation is re-established.” Clarify how this measure is consistent with

                                   6
      sections III.E and V.A.6 of the FERC Plan (beneficial reuse) and indicate if
     this measure was recommended by a land managing agency and/or state
     resource agency.

e.   Section 4.3.2 states “during clearing operations, where feasible based on
     topographic conditions and available workspace, Arizona protected native
     plant species will be avoided along the edges of the construction rights-of-
     way.” Clarify why these measures would not also be implemented in Texas
     and New Mexico.

f.   Section 4.3.6 states “The contractor will backfill and stabilize areas as soon
     as possible according to Transwestern’s FERC Plan (Section V.A.1.) which
     specifies that final grading topsoil replacement and installation of
     permanent erosion control structures will be completed within 35 days after
     backfilling the trench.” (emphasis added). Include the following additional
     information.

        i. We note that Transwestern’s FERC Plan at section V.A.1 does not
           state that final grading, topsoil replacement, and installation of
           permanent erosion control structures “will” be completed within 35
           days after backfilling the trench, but rather “Transwestern will
           endeavor to complete” these activities within that time. Clarify this
           apparent discrepancy.

        ii. Transwestern’s FERC Plan at section V.A.1 states “Transwestern
            requests additional time (15 days) to complete final cleanup due to
            the Project’s extent and remoteness and the topographic conditions
            in some areas.” Clarify why advanced planning for these conditions
            would not be sufficient to allow for Transwestern to complete final
            cleanup within 20 days of backfilling the trench, especially in
            consideration of Transwestern’s FERC Plan at section III.A.3, which
            indicates Transwestern would plan construction sequencing to limit
            the amount and duration of open trench segments.

g.   Section 5.1.4 mentions that a soil tackifier may be used in lieu of straw or
     hydromulch within 100 feet of waterbodies/dry washes. Identify soil
     tackifiers that may be used, include associated safety data sheets, and
     describe any consultations with land management agencies or landowners
     regarding use of these products in these areas.


                                    7
 h.   Section 6.0 states “if dry washes are flowing, Transwestern will limit the
     number of such crossings of each waterbody to one per piece of
     equipment.” We note that this proposed measure would not be consistent
     with section V.B.5.a and V.B.7.b of the FERC Procedures, which limits
     crossing of waterbodies with flow to “only clearing equipment and
     equipment necessary for installation of equipment bridges" or only
     equipment needed to construct the crossing (for minor waterbodies).
     Revise this text to be consistent with the FERC Procedures or include this
     measure as a requested modification to the FERC Procedure (refer to
     question 24).

i.   Section 6.0 states “Contractors may utilize other alternatives for equipment
     bridges that achieve the same performance and objectives, where approved
     by Transwestern…Transwestern’s EI or Representative will review all
     bridge placements to verify bridge safety and ensure the performance
     standards are observed so that resource effects are minimized to the extent
     practical based on site-specific crossing conditions and engineering
     constraints.” Include a statement confirming that the EI would also verify
     that use of an equipment bridge alternative would not result in
     environmental effects not analyzed previously, e.g., adverse effects on
     protected species.

j.   Section 9.0 describes that hydrostatic test water release rates “would be
     controlled to prevent scour, erosion, and potential effects or sediment
     migration into sensitive resources or facilities.” Revise Section 9.0 to
     address the following additional information/clarification:

        i. in accordance with the FERC Procedures at section VII.B.3, file a
           list identifying the location of all dry washes proposed for use as a
           hydrostatic test water source discharge locations;

        ii. in accordance with the FERC Procedures at section VII.D.1,
            additionally confirm that Transwestern would regulate discharge
            rate, use energy dissipation device(s), and install sediment barriers,
            as necessary, to prevent streambed scour, suspension of sediments,
            or excessive streamflow during discharge to dry washes;

       iii. clarify the permitting requirements for discharge into a waterbody;
            and


                                    8
        iv. Figure 14 does not depict a dewatering structure. Figure 13 shows a
           dewatering structure for hydrostatic testing with a label indicating
           “well vegetated area (if possible).” Given the sparse vegetation in
           an arid climate and that Transwestern acknowledged that discharge
           rate is based on a number of factors, including “contractor means
           and methods,” further clarify how Transwestern would ensure that
           discharge of hydrostatic test water and dewatering comply with
           above commitments.

k.   Section 9.0 states, regarding the release of hydrostatic test water and trench
     dewatering activities, “the EIs will ensure that turbid water is not
     discharged to waters of the state.” Include confirmation that, in accordance
     with the FERC Procedures at section V.B.11, Transwestern would conduct
     trench dewatering “in a manner that does not cause erosion and does not
     result in silt-laden water flowing into any waterbody” (not just waters of the
     state).

l.   Section 11.0 states “Waterbody crossings will be stabilized and temporary
     sediment barriers will be installed within 24 hours of completion of
     backfilling.” Include confirmation that in accordance with section V.C.2 of
     the FERC Procedures, Transwestern would “for open-cut crossings,
     stabilize waterbody banks and install temporary sediment barriers within 24
     hours of completing instream construction activities.”

m.   Section 11.2 states “during final cleanup, all construction debris (e.g., mats,
     garbage, drilling fluids) will be cleared from the right-of-way and disposed
     of in accordance with state and local regulations.” Include confirmation
     that in accordance with the FERC Plan at section III.E, Transwestern would
     "determine methods and locations for the regular collection, containment,
     and disposal of excess construction materials and debris...throughout the
     construction process” (i.e., not just during final cleanup).

n.   Section 2.5 of the Noxious Weed and Invasive Plant Management Plan
     (attachment E of Transwestern’s ECRP), states that cleared vegetation with
     noxious and invasive weeds would be stockpiled and “returned to the
     infestation sites from which they were stripped or moved.” Revise to
     clarify how this measure is consistent with sections III.F.1 and III.E of the
     FERC Plan (beneficial reuse) and indicate if this measure was
     recommended by a land managing agency and/or state resource agency.

                                    9
 Resource Report 5

31.   Resolve apparent inconsistencies between the Estimated Workforce and Schedule
      discussion in Resource Report 1 (section 1.5) and the information presented in
      Resource Report 5, such as:

       a.    Resource Report 1 describes the Spread 1 to 4 workforce peak as August to
             November 2028 whereas Resource Report 5 indicates July to
             November/December 2028; and

       b.    Resource Report 1 describes the Spread 5A to 5B peak as August to
             November 2028 while Resource Report 5 indicates August 2028 to
             February 2029.

32.   The analysis in Resource Report 5 includes Yavapai County, Arizona, where the
      Ash Fork regulator station would be located. For clarity, include a reference to
      this county in the introductory text of section 5.2.

33.   Clarify that the project area discussed in the first paragraph of section 5.2.1 is for
      the mainline. Laterals and compression stations would extend farther west into
      Maricopa and Mojave Counties, Arizona.

34.   Check numbers in tables for typos, including:

       a.    table 5.2-22 – see Hidalgo row, total sales $31.957; Maricopa row,
             livestock $815.425; and

       b.    table 5.2-24 – see Homeowner Vacancy Rate, Hidalgo County, 3/0%.

35.   Some trauma center designations in table 5.2-27 appear to be incorrect. For
      example, Pima County has only two Level 1 trauma centers: Banner University
      Medical Center Main Campus (not listed) and St. Joseph’s Hospital. St. Mary’s
      Hospital is not Level 1 (see
      https://www.azdhs.gov/documents/preparedness/emergency-medical-services-
      trauma-system/trauma/az-designated-trauma-centers.pdf). Check other counties
      and make corrections as needed.

36.   In section 5.2.5, clarify that the laterals would go as far as Mohave County,
      Arizona.




                                             10
 37.   Identify specific traffic management measures that Transwestern would use to
      minimize traffic effects on local roadways.

38.   Resolve the following issues in tables:

       a.    Table 5.2-3 – explain (e.g., with table note) dashes for Hudspeth and El
             Paso Counties. Do they mean no oil and gas production, or no data
             available.

       b.    Table 5.2-26 – explain why some of the Texas and New Mexico counties
             crossed by the project are not included.

       c.    Table 5.2-27 – explain why some of the Texas counties crossed by the
             project are not included.

       d.    Table 5.2-31 – explain why the New Mexico entries include a “Remainder
             of county” line, but the Texas and Arizona entries do not.

       e.    Table 5A-1 – add City of Tucson Environmental Services and Waste
             Management in the Pima County row for sanitation.

        f.   Table 5A-4 – text may be missing (see missing parentheses) and data
             misaligned in the rows for Doña Ana County and Maricopa County.

       g.    Table 5A-6 – for the Reeves County row, add the missing spread number in
             the second column.

Resource Report 10

39.   Table 10.4-1 identifies that El Paso Natural Gas’s (EPNG) existing pipelines
      provide natural gas to or “near” the existing/proposed facilities that would receive
      natural gas from the Apache, San Manuel, Saguaro, Germann, and Harquahala
      Laterals. Transwestern states it “assumes” the EPNG system would need to be
      upgraded to provide additional natural gas. Clarify, as known, if the EPNG
      system does or does not have sufficient available capacity to meet Project need for
      each of these laterals.

40.   Assess the Green Chile Lateral (FERC Docket No. CP26-80) as a system
      alternative to the Red Chile Lateral. Describe the modifications that would be
      required for the Green Chile Lateral to provide proposed capacity of the Red Chile
      Lateral.


                                           11
 41.   Identify in table 10.4-1, as applicable, where the purpose of Project laterals is to
      diversify natural gas supply to the respective end-use facilities.

42.   Section 1.4.1.1 states “Transwestern has designed a typical 150-foot-wide
      temporary construction right-of-way for the 48-inch diameter
      mainline…narrowing the right-of-way width and eliminating the travel lane would
      significantly restrict traffic flow along the right-of-way, and efficient traffic flow
      minimizes impacts by reducing the number of access roads that may need to be
      constructed.” As previously requested, include a comparison of effects where
      narrower rights-of-way with alternative access approaches were considered. More
      specifically, assess an alternative for the mainline that eliminates the bi-directional
      travel lane in the construction right-of-way and uses additional access roads
      instead. The analysis should include, but not be limited to, a quantitative
      comparison of the estimated land required (e.g., acres).

43.   Table 10.5-5 refers to a proposed and preferred CS5-Lordsburg location and a
      proposed and preferred route alternative. To avoid confusion, revise this and other
      similar text to clearly indicate which locations or routes are being proposed, i.e.,
      avoid using both “proposed” and “preferred” terminology.

44.   Clarify the apparent conflicting mileposts (MP) for Construction Optimization
      Alternative 1 in section 10.5.1.9. Alternative 1 is described both as being between
      MPs 443.4 and 460.6 and as starting from MP 443.2 and ending at MP 463.2.

45.   Section 10.5.2.3 evaluates route alternatives affecting the Lower Gila Terraces and
      Historic Trails Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC). Transwestern
      states Alternative 1 was considered prior to development of the proposed route,
      and notes that Alternative 1 does not terminate at the customer’s final
      development design location. Evaluate a modified Alternative 1, including
      mapping and comparative analysis, that terminates at the customer’s final
      development design location. For portions of the modified route that would
      continue to cross the ACEC, identify and discuss specific construction techniques
      (e.g., reduced-width open cut, trenchless crossing techniques, etc.) that minimize
      the effects on the ACEC. If an identified minimization measure is not technically
      feasible or practicable, explain why.

46.   Assess alternative routes suggested in the comments on the Project, including:




                                            12
        a.   Accession No. 20260716-5119 - route the mainline adjacent to the existing
            Union Pacific Railroad right-of-way through Coolidge.

       b.   Accession No. 20260805-5230 - shift the mainline route approximately 0.5
            mile south, nearer to the two existing gas pipelines and away from both
            existing and future residences.

       c.    Accession No. 20260803-5133 - evaluate reasonable route alternatives and
            mitigation measures that avoid or minimize effects on Insignia property,
            including alternatives that use existing infrastructure corridors, avoid
            planned access and utility areas, follow property boundaries where
            practicable, and preserve the property’s independent developability.

       d.   Accession Nos. 20260804-5072, 20260805-5050, and 20260804-5085 -
            assess a reasonable route alternative that minimizes effects on the property
            indicated in the comments.

       e.   Accession No. 20260805-5165 - assess reasonable route alternatives that
            avoid or minimize effects on active ranching operations (including C-Spear
            Ranch) and environmentally sensitive areas within the San Pedro River
            Valley. For the evaluation consider effects on livestock operations, grazing
            management, water resources, wildlife habitat, and private property rights.

       f.   Accession No. 20261009-5001 - assess the feasibility of a minor route
            alternative closer to the southern boundary of the referenced property.

47.   In section 10.5.1.7, Transwestern commits to developing management,
      monitoring, and mitigation plans with the U.S. Bureau of Land Management and
      The Nature Conservancy. Describe the status of those plans and identify the
      specific measures under consideration.
